newsitem.title: UK: World wonders what happens to China if Deng dies.
newsitem.headline: World wonders what happens to China if Deng dies.

text.p: By Nicholas Doughty, Diplomatic Correspondent
What will happen to China if paramount leader Deng Xiaoping really is on his deathbed?

The outside world is struggling with the implications of a power shift in China and what it could mean for stability in a region that has become increasingly nervous about Asia's mightiest power, with its 1.2 billion people.
Beijing is playing down reports that the 92-year-old Deng, architect of the economic reforms that have turned China into a powerhouse, may finally be close to death.

Nevertheless, diplomats and analysts say, China must now face important questions about its future -- and they say Deng's death would enable this debate to come into the open since his decisive influence will be gone.

The immediate transition of power is likely to be relatively smooth, at least on the surface, since Western experts say Communist Party chief Jiang Zemin has prepared the ground carefully to take on the role as Deng's successor.

"The fact that Deng has been ailing for so long has done a lot for stability in China, because it has allowed political realignment to come at a steady pace," said Bates Gill of the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI).
"There is a succession formally in place and so it may not make a lot of difference for a few months," said Gerald Segal of London's International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS).

Jiang, who is also state president and head of the army, has taken care to build up a solid power base after a shaky start when he was first promoted in the wake of the 1989 Tiananmen Square massacre.
While his stature does not even approach the reverence accorded to Deng, he is certainly seen as the first among equals in the leadership.
Beyond that, things become less clear.
Deng's death would force current debates within China's
political elite about the direction of economic policy, political control and foreign affairs into the open at a time of radical, breakneck change.

These may or may not be resolved in time for the Communist Party's 15th Congress, likely to be held in October. Positions on the central committee and control of key ministries could all be up for grabs.
The country's ruling elite faces fundamental questions.
Will China continue to practise its hybrid of economic

liberalism, huge state industries and authoritarian political control? Will those who believe more law and order is necessary to beat corruption and the erosion of central power win out, and will there be trouble if they slow things down?
Will China embrace Western-style capitalism
wholeheartedly, pushing reforms harder and faster than before, and what about the risk of social unrest in doing so? What would this mean for the Communist Party itself?
"The leadership has to manage the process of radical
change that has been started, that is the fundamental problem for the next five to 10 years," said Segal.
"The tensions inherent in their system are not sustainable in the long-term. They have to make decisions about where reforms are going."
"There is a very vigorous debate going on about this already but it has to stay unresolved until Deng dies," said one Western diplomat with detailed knowledge of China.
"China will face problems whichever path it chooses."
While economic liberalisation has delivered stunning growth, it has also brought increased social problems, including crime, corruption and unemployment.

Some coastal and southern regions have boomed, acquiring real power and money in the process. Many rural areas -- where most of China's people live -- remain backward and people are flooding into already overburdened cities. The country is increasingly fragmented.
No one in the Chinese leadership can afford to look
weak or risk embarrassment while this debate rages, especially with key positions to play for in a post-Deng China.
As a result, there has been a crackdown on dissent at

home and Chinese foreign policy has already become more assertive -- missile launches to intimidate Taiwan last year, a tough line on Hong Kong before Britain hands it back and trouble with the United States on trade and human rights.
Michael Yahuda, a leading China expert at the London
School of Economics (LSE), believes there will be little change in this tough approach at home and abroad after Deng dies.
"These lesser men, as they are by comparison with Deng,
are going to feel more at risk," he told Reuters. "They will be ultra-cautious and we'll probably see a less flexible approach until they feel things have settled."
